books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, 1835

stimulus.text:
Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835), on the peoples of the United States:

“Three races naturally distinct, and I might almost say hostile to each other, are discoverable among them at the first glance. ... fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfils its destiny apart.”

“As soon as it is admitted that the whites and the emancipated blacks are placed upon the same territory in the situation of two alien communities, it will readily be understood that there are but two alternatives for the future; the negroes and the whites must either wholly part or wholly mingle.”

“I do not imagine that the white and black races will ever live in any country upon an equal footing.”

Background: Tocqueville, a French visitor, traveled in the United States in 1831–1832 and published Democracy in America in 1835.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18 (Reeve translation, 1835), public domain, as printed on Wikisource.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18 (1835), public domain
stem: Tocqueville wrote in 1835, when the Missouri Compromise still held and abolitionism was young. Why does his warning matter for understanding the rest of Period 4?

options.text: He named slavery as the danger that could break the Union
He predicted the exact year the Union would break
options.misconception: Tocqueville gave no date; he warned about a danger, not a calendar.

options.text: He proved that the North and South had no economic ties
options.misconception: The North and South were deeply tied by cotton and trade.

options.text: He showed that Native peoples would soon govern the West
options.misconception: Tocqueville described hardship for Native peoples, not power.

rationales.A: He looked past tariffs and trade to the three races. Slavery was the divide he thought could break the Union.
rationales.B: No year appears in the passage. Tocqueville warns of a danger, not a date.
rationales.C: The regions were tied together by cotton, mills, and trade. Tocqueville never says otherwise.
rationales.D: The passage gives Native peoples no such future. Tocqueville writes of their suffering and decline.
rationales.general:
1. Note the date. Tocqueville wrote in 1835, before Texas, before the Mexican War, before the fiercest slavery fights.
2. Ask what he saw early. He saw three peoples who did not mix, and slavery as the divide between two of them.
3. Name why it matters. The fights of the 1840s over new land were the danger he had already named.
Background: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 had postponed the slavery question, not settled it.
Remember: an early warning matters when later events follow the path it traced.
